Function description and modelling clues¶

What the fitted comparisons add¶

The local GP has held-out MAE 0.03686, versus 0.05953 for the mean baseline. The quadratic is worse than that baseline. This favours local modelling over assuming one broad quadratic shape among the methods examined.

The prediction error is much larger than the gap between the two best measured scores, so their fine ranking does not locate a resolved optimum. The current UCB point (0.658460, 0.558234, 0.006012) explores a low-x3 region outside the full 3D sampled hull. Its predicted mean is -0.031223 and SD is 0.078202; the positive UCB 0.122053 is an acquisition score, not a predicted positive return. The description supplies no exact noise level or proven attainable optimum.

Held-out comparisons and method selection use the same small snapshot; they are not independent final-test results. The notes do not change targets, settings or query policies.

2. Learn the picture before using it on the black box¶

The blue line is the GP's posterior mean: its central prediction after seeing observations. The pale band is mean plus or minus 1.96 standard deviations: a pointwise interval for the latent function under the model's assumptions. It is not a simultaneous guarantee for the whole curve, and it excludes fresh observation noise. Green crosses are measured values at the displayed inputs.

Only in this invented one-input example can we also draw the orange dashed known function. The three panels use 3, 6 and 10 points from a fixed invented sequence. They demonstrate updating a model, not a query-selection policy. None of these points uses the course query allowance. The GP's kernel, noise level and prior scale stay fixed across the panels.

The same visual convention is used in scikit-learn's introductory GP example. For the actual black box we have observations and predictions, but no known orange truth curve.

In the real three-input function, the curve below will become a path through the input cube. Two input coordinates must be held fixed before that path can be drawn against an output axis.

3. Choose the target scale and a reference input¶

All 18 current outputs are negative, ranging from about -0.399 to -0.035. Raw outputs are readable on this range. Retain every sign and value; a less negative output is a higher score. The GP means, standard deviations, validation errors and acquisition scores are therefore in raw output units.

Use the best observed input as a reference for the paths and sections that follow. It is the best of these observations, not a known optimum. Holding its other coordinates fixed lets us repeat the same GP picture along each input direction without confusing a projection with a slice.

4. Compare the same models, using all three inputs¶

  • Mean baseline: predict the average of the training outputs, ignoring inputs.
  • Linear ridge: fit a three-input plane with a coefficient penalty.
  • Quadratic ridge: fit three linear terms, three squares and three pairwise interactions, plus an intercept.
  • Local GP: use an RBF length scale of 0.15 in the three-input space.
  • Broad GP: repeat with length scale 0.35.

The ridge penalties remain alpha=1.0. Both GPs assume noise SD of 10% of the training output SD, normalise targets within each fit and keep their declared kernel settings fixed. The extra input contributes to distance: reusing a 2D length scale does not establish that it is appropriate in 3D. These are a small set of stated hypotheses rather than an optimisation over model settings.

Leave-one-out (LOO) hides each result and fits the complete estimator on the other 17 rows. Feature scaling is refitted inside each fold. Lower MAE or RMSE is better; an MAE ratio below 1 beats the training-mean baseline. With 23 observations and ten quadratic coefficients including the intercept, smooth fitted surfaces can still predict hidden results poorly.

5. Locate three one-dimensional paths in the input cube¶

The next cloud uses x1, x2, x3 as its three axes and measured output as colour. Three straight paths intersect at the best observed input. Each varies one coordinate while keeping the other two fixed. Drag the cube to see the paths from different angles.

The following response curves use output, rather than another input, on their vertical axis. They are predictions along these paths. There is no known orange truth curve for the actual black box.

6. Repeat the mean, band and observations in every direction¶

Each column varies one named input and holds the other two at the reference values in its title. The rows compare local and broad GPs; all six panels share output limits. The blue curve is the GP mean, the pale area is its pointwise 95% latent-function band under the declared assumptions, and green crosses are measurements matching both held coordinates.

Other observations still inform the joint GP but are not projected onto these paths. Bands exclude fresh observation noise and uncertainty about the model itself. They can express confidence under assumptions that the held-out checks do not support. The paths span the input interval, including locations outside the sampled hull.

7. From a curve to a plane of contour lines¶

A plane varies two inputs and fixes the third. A contour joins points on that plane with the same fitted output. Its level is an output value, not an observation rank or an uncertainty measure. Closely spaced contours indicate a steeper change in this model's fitted output.

The quadratic contains all three inputs jointly:

$$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1x_1 + b_2x_2 + b_3x_3 + b_4x_1^2 + b_5x_1x_2 + b_6x_1x_3 + b_7x_2^2 + b_8x_2x_3 + b_9x_3^2.$$

The contour matrix repeats the earlier quadratic study at held-coordinate values 0.25, 0.50, 0.75. All panels share colours and levels. Masking uses the full 3D sampled hull, not the projected outline of an input pair. Blank regions are outside that hull; remaining interior gaps and model uncertainty still matter. Measurements at different held coordinates are not drawn on these planes.

8. Compare models on the same sections; rotate the fitted terrain¶

Use a second contour matrix to compare the quadratic and local GP on the three planes through the reference input. Each column varies the same pair in both rows, holding the third at the same value. Shared colours allow direct comparison of the fitted output. Neither row is the true function.

The draggable quadratic terrain retains the three pairwise panels and held-input slider. Its vertical axis is fitted output; one input is supplied by the slider. All three held inputs move to the same slider value. It uses a 31 x 31 display grid, sampled from the finer 61 x 61 calculations, and sends only updated heights in each frame. This reduces rendering work while retaining flat 0.16 vertical proportions. A blank panel has no intersection with the sampled hull at that value.

9. Separate a high mean from high uncertainty¶

Repeat the mean, standard deviation and upper confidence bound on those three planes:

$$\operatorname{UCB}(x) = \mu(x) + \kappa\sigma(x), \qquad \kappa = 1.96.$$

UCB is an acquisition score, not a predicted output or a guarantee of improvement. The weight is a declared heuristic. Each row fixes its titled coordinate and varies the two axis inputs. Colours are shared down each column; mean, SD and UCB use their own scales.

These score panels colour the entire plane to reveal uncertainty outside the sampled hull. The dotted boundary is the intersection with the full 3D hull. A plane with no such intersection is entirely extrapolation. Black dots are only observations whose held coordinate matches the plane. The actual coverage point generally lies on different planes, so it is evaluated in a table and shown in a separate 3D cloud below rather than misleadingly projected here.

10. If we switched today: a hypothetical model-led next query¶

Choose the lower-LOO-MAE GP among the two fixed GP comparisons, then maximise mean + 1.96 * SD over 4,096 seeded three-dimensional Sobol points plus the eight allowed extreme corners. Round coordinates to six decimals before predicting, remove duplicates and already observed coordinates, then score those exact inputs. The winner is the best of this finite pool, not a proven continuous optimum. Candidates outside the sampled hull are permitted and labelled.

A GP is used here because this rule needs both a mean and uncertainty; the lowest-error model overall may be a different regressor. The chosen GP's MAE ratio is printed beside the suggestion. A ratio of 1 or more means it does not beat the mean baseline. The weight sensitivity table reuses the same predictions, with no additional fits or course evaluations. This hypothetical policy leaves the saved coverage decision unchanged.

The proposed mean is compared with the best measured output. UCB can select a point with a lower mean because its uncertainty may make it informative; a high score does not predict a new best result.

11. Locate the hypothetical point without flattening away an input¶

The cloud puts actual coverage and hypothetical GP-UCB inputs at their real three-dimensional coordinates. Both are unevaluated: their fixed marker colours do not represent measured outputs. Drag to inspect their relationship with the observations.

Then repeat the mean, SD and UCB panels on three planes through the hypothetical point. Each panel holds the third coordinate at the proposal's value, so its magenta X really belongs to that section. The actual coverage point is not projected onto these planes. Read the held values and hull intersections before interpreting a colourful peak.

Read the pictures in the same order each time¶

  1. Identify which axes are inputs and which visual quantity represents output.
  2. For a curve, name both held inputs; for a contour map, name the held third input.
  3. Read the fitted mean, then its model band or SD, and compare held-out errors with the mean baseline.
  4. Check whether the location is inside the full 3D sampled hull or is an extrapolation.
  5. Separate measured results, a model's suggested query and the actual coverage policy.

The black box remains unknown. A narrow band, smooth contour or high UCB does not establish a real optimum. The comparisons use 23 observations, including any model-selection choices made here. For Week 4, the exploration notebook's saved coverage sequence remains the original query decision.
